SK3042 The double-checked locking is not correct

A check-lock-check initialization reads its field outside the lock and the field is not volatile.

CategoryAsync
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3

Why

The idiom exists to skip the lock on the common path, and the read it skips the lock for is the outer one. Without volatile nothing orders that read against the writes the constructor performed, so a second thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose fields it cannot see yet, and use it. The lock is real, the inner check is real, and the object is still half-built. ⚠ It works on x86 and x64 by accident of those processors' ordering and stops working on ARM64, which is where a great deal of .NET now runs — so this is not a fragile shape, it is a shape with a platform on which it is already wrong.

Example

Instead of:

static Settings? instance;

public static Settings Instance {
    get {
        if (instance == null) {
            lock (Gate) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new Settings();
                }
            }
        }

        return instance;
    }
}

Write:

static volatile Settings? instance;

public static Settings Instance {
    get {
        if (instance == null) {
            lock (Gate) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new Settings();
                }
            }
        }

        return instance;
    }
}

When it does not fire

⚠ Fixless. Adding volatile looks like a one-word edit and is not one: it changes the field's memory contract for every access in the program, costs a fence on every read of a field that may be read in a loop, and is only one of three defensible repairs — the others being Lazy<T> (see SK3009) and dropping the outer check for an unconditional lock. Choosing among those is a design decision. ⚠ The shape is gated four ways and all four must hold: the outer condition is the whole condition and a plain field reference tested for null (or !flag on a bool field); its body runs a lock; the lock body holds a second check of the same field; and that second branch publishes the field with a plain assignment. Volatile.Read(ref f) == null fails the first gate and Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref f, …) fails the last, which is how code that has already done the ordering by hand stays silent. ⚠ Reference types and `bool` only. The finding's advice is "make it volatile", and CS0677 makes that illegal for long, double, decimal and any user struct, so on those the message would name a repair that does not compile. ⚠ The field must be declared in source, because a field from another assembly cannot be made volatile by anybody reading the finding. ⚠ Two of the three ReSharper inspections named in the proposing issue are not covered: PossibleMultipleWriteAccessInDoubleCheckLocking and ReadAccessInDoubleCheckLocking both turn on distinguishing f = new Foo(); f.Init(); from var t = new Foo(); t.Init(); f = t;, and separating those from a harmless return f; in the same branch needs a rule about which reads publish. Stated rather than approximated. ⚠ A single-threaded type that happens to be written this way is reported; the idiom's whole point is threading, so the shape is its own claim about intent.
